# Actor {#sec-actor}

[Hands, and a circuit that chooses what they do]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="2.5"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** hands. A creature picks a berry from a bush, holds it, and then eats it or puts it down. And the
basal ganglia's *actor*: for each hand action a pair of striatal cells, one that releases the action and one that
holds it back, taught by the critic's dopamine.

**Result:** creatures with the actor live better than creatures without it, and they use what the actor learns.
In a world where the poison bushes have thorns, they learn within their lives to leave the thorny bushes, and the
actor's learning keeps them picking the good ones. Without its learning the actor still works, but costs them a fifth of
their fitness, in one line up to two fifths.
:::

Until now biting a bush was eating it. In this stage the two come apart: the action USE picks a berry with an empty
hand and puts it down with a full one, and EAT eats what is held. **The same action now means different things in
different situations**, and the right one depends on what is in hand. That is the job of an actor: a circuit that
learns, from the critic's surprise, which action pays where.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="2.5"></div>

## The circuit

- **Hands.** The pallium reads what is in hand as well as what is ahead, so the critic and the actor know what is
  held. Appetite and aversion now mean *eat it* and *do not eat it*: cells about the held berry drive and stop
  swallowing (`ingest`, `no_eat`), and a berry in hand is swallowed by default unless aversion stops it. The old
  programmes about what is seen act on eating as well; evolution may take them away entirely.
- **The actor** has one channel per hand action, USE and EAT. In each, a *Go* cell (`striatum_d1`) and a *NoGo* cell
  (`striatum_d2`) read the pallium. Go inhibits the steadily active output cell (`gpi`), which releases the action's
  programme (`act`); NoGo inhibits a relay (`gpe`) that otherwise holds `gpi` down, so NoGo strengthens the brake.
- **Learning.** A dopamine burst strengthens the synapses onto Go cells that were active a moment before, a pause
  those onto NoGo cells. Which cells were active is marked by a copy of the action just taken, sent back to the
  striatum (an *efference copy*), so an action is credited also when an older circuit chose it.
- **A start.** A full hand releases USE now and then, so that putting down is tried at all and can be learned.
  Evolution sets how often.
- **Nothing new for the thorns.** A prick is a pain like a snake bite, felt by the pain cells the critic already
  reads; the brain is the same as without thorns.

## Biology

The dorsal striatum is the input of the basal ganglia. Its cells come in two kinds with two dopamine receptors. D1
cells form the *direct* pathway: they inhibit the output nuclei (GPi, SNr), whose steady inhibition holds the
brainstem's motor programmes shut, and so release an action. D2 cells form the *indirect* pathway through the
external pallidum and hold it back. Dopamine bursts strengthen the active synapses onto D1 cells and pauses those
onto D2 cells, so actions that turned out better than expected are released more readily and worse ones held back.
With the critic of the last page this is the *actor-critic* of reinforcement learning, and the basal ganglia are its
best-known biological counterpart.

The two pathways are old: lampreys, the oldest living vertebrate line, have them, with the same transmitters and
dopamine receptors. That the striatum gets a copy of the motor command is clearest in songbirds, where a basal
ganglia loop learns which variant of a song syllable was sung when the song turned out well.

Learning to leave defended prey alone is old too. Pike that snap at three-spined sticklebacks get their mouths
pricked by the spines and soon stop attacking them, while still taking minnows; toads stung by a bee stop
snapping at bees, and at the flies that look like them.

## The world

The critic's harsh world, without the switch: one berry to a bush, a poison berry costing as much food as a good one
gives, small meals and a slow metabolism. Eating now takes a hand: a berry must be picked, then eaten. A held berry
blocks the next pick until it is eaten or put down, and it can only be put down on an empty cell.

**The poison bushes have thorns** (not in OHOL, though real gooseberry bushes are spiny). Picking from one pricks: a
small pain and a little food lost, at the pick itself, before anything is eaten. Which kinds are poison, and so
thorny, is drawn anew for every life, so it has to be learned each time.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="2.5"></div>

## Did it work?

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="2.5" data-used="act,no_plasticity,learn_off:striatum_d1"></div>

**The actor pays.** Creatures with it live longer well fed than creatures without it, alone and when the two kinds
share a world, and less of what they eat is poison. The lead is smaller in one of the three lines, where the
creatures without the actor had learned to leave the thorny bushes alone almost completely.

**And they lean on its learning.** Switching off the learning of the actor's Go cells costs about a fifth of the
fitness (a tenth to two fifths per line), that of the NoGo cells about a tenth. Silencing the actor's output (`act`)
costs a third.

### In the lab

One creature at a time is put in a box, 48 times: in front of a bush with an empty hand, or with a berry in hand
and nothing ahead. Which two of the four kinds are poison, and thorny, is new for every creature, so whatever it
does with them after the first trials it has learned.

<div data-life="lines" data-stage="2.5" data-example="pick_curve"></div>

**The actor keeps the good bushes picked.** Creatures with the actor learn to leave the thorny bushes (from about
seven in ten picked to four) and go on picking more than eight in ten of the good ones. With the striatum's learning
switched off they leave the thorny bushes just as well, through the cells of appetite and aversion, but the good
ones come along: fewer and fewer of them are picked. The prick spreads to everything that looks like a bush, and
what the actor learns, from the good berries that follow a pick, holds that back. Creatures without the actor leave
the thorny bushes almost completely, but also four in ten of the good ones from the start.

<div data-life="lines" data-stage="2.5" data-example="hold_curve"></div>

**A poison berry in hand is put down.** At first a creature with the actor swallows a poison berry it holds; within
a dozen trials it puts most of them down instead, with or without the striatum's learning: that what is not
swallowed gets put down is built in. Creatures without the actor cannot put anything down: they hold the berry, and often
swallow it in the end.

**Why thorns.** Without them a wrong pick cost nothing the critic could see: the creature found the berry bad and put
it down, a few ticks lost. The actor's circuit was used then, but its learning was not (a few percent at most). A
prick is a cost of the action itself, which the cells about eating cannot prevent: only picking less can.
Thorns on every bush were tried first. They failed: a creature that cannot yet tell the kinds apart loses food on
every pick, and a prick after every pick taught aversion to every colour.

The old programmes about what is seen (`grasp`, `no_feed`) are not needed any more. Neither is the aversion to the
berry in hand (`no_eat`): with the poison bushes picked less, a poison berry is seldom held.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The lab in numbers"}
<div data-life="table" data-stage="2.5" data-example="hand_lab"></div>
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What it took"}
- **The berry has to tell something new.** In a first version every kind's bush, berry and empty bush shared one
  colour, and creatures picked and ate at once, as if eating were still biting: the berry in hand said nothing the
  bush had not. A world where only the berries were coloured was tried and dropped.
- **Valence means eating.** First the cells about what is seen still worked on USE, as they had when picking was
  eating. A creature that had learned to dislike a poison berry in hand then could not put it down: the dislike
  stopped the hand. On EAT, where appetite and aversion belong, USE is the actor's.
- **No switch.** The critic's world swapped poison and good kinds halfway through every life. Here a berry that is
  refused is never tasted again, so a dislike learned before the swap never faded, and both kinds ended up disliked.
  The switch was there to show the critic at work and is gone from this stage on.
- **A fresh start for the hands.** In the critic stage the hand was always empty and EAT did nothing, so the
  synapses from the held senses and onto EAT had drifted unselected; they start silent. Swallowing what is held
  is the default, with a strength that evolves.
- **The right moment.** The cells of appetite and aversion read the pallium of the same tick, not of the tick
  before: a berry is swallowed on its first tick in hand, before a lesson a tick late could stop it.
- **Room to remove.** The connections of the old programmes that got in the way can be evolved down to nothing,
  not only weakened.
- **A cost for a wrong pick.** Without one the actor's learning was not used (the stage was first frozen so). Thorns
  on every bush starved the creatures at the start, at every setting tried; thorns on the poison bushes only, a
  small pain and a little food, let the start live and made picking by look pay.
- **Fifty generations**, not a hundred: the difference between the two kinds was clear by generation 20 to 30.
:::
